prompt: `laptop` captured everything to or from `files` for five seconds while `files` fetched a page from `web1`. Both are on the same switch. What did the capture hold?
hint: Where does a switch send a unicast frame?

choices.text: The whole HTTP exchange, request and page
choices.why: A switch sends a unicast frame out of one port; the page never reached the laptop's.

choices.text: Only the SYN that opened the connection
choices.why: The SYN is unicast too, from files to its gateway, and went nowhere near the laptop.

choices.text: One ARP request, which is a broadcast
choices.why: Right. A broadcast goes out of every port, so it was the only thing the laptop could see.

choices.text: Nothing, because the laptop was not on a mirror port
choices.why: It did capture one packet: a port that is not a mirror still receives broadcasts.

prompt: `mon` captured the whole conversation on the mirror port without an IP address. Why does it need none?
hint: Is mon part of the conversation?

choices.text: The switch lends it the address of the mirrored port
choices.why: A switch lends no addresses; it copies frames.

choices.text: It sends nothing and is sent nothing; it reads copies
choices.why: Right. An address is for taking part, and mon only listens.

choices.text: tshark gives the interface a temporary address while capturing
choices.why: tshark assigns nothing; the interface stayed unaddressed.

choices.text: Members of the wireshark group may capture without one
choices.why: The group is about permission to capture, not about addressing.

prompt: A busy 10 Gbit/s uplink is mirrored to an analyser on a 1 Gbit/s port. The capture shows gaps where acknowledgements refer to data that is not in the file. What is the first explanation to rule out?
hint: Where can a copy be lost?

choices.text: The network is losing packets between the two hosts
choices.why: The acknowledgements say the data arrived; what is missing is the copy.

choices.text: A display filter is hiding part of the traffic
choices.why: Clearing a display filter brings everything back, and would be checked in a second anyway.

choices.text: The switch dropped copies it had no room for on the mirror port
choices.why: Right. Ten gigabits do not fit into one, and the loss happens on the way to the analyser.

choices.text: The analyser is not in the wireshark group
choices.why: Without permission it would capture nothing at all, not most of the traffic.

prompt: Match each place to capture from with what it gives you.
hint: One of them depends on the switch's configuration.

pairs.right: Copies of one port or VLAN, set up on the switch
Both directions of one cable, whatever the switch does
Everything that one machine sends and receives

right_distractors: Every unicast frame of the LAN, from any ordinary port

prompt: Why could `ana` run `tshark -i eth0` on `mon` without `sudo`?
hint: Look at id -nG.

choices.text: tshark needs no privilege to capture
choices.why: Capturing does need one; lesson 12 shows tcpdump refused without it.

choices.text: mon has no address, so nothing on it is protected
choices.why: Permissions on a machine do not depend on its addresses.

choices.text: She is in the wireshark group
choices.why: Right. The package lets that group run the helper that opens the interface.

choices.text: tshark only ever reads files
choices.why: It captured live from eth0 in the same lesson.

prompt: What is gained by capturing as a member of a group rather than running the whole analyser as root?
hint: Which code reads what strangers send?

choices.text: The dissectors that parse untrusted packets run without privileges
choices.why: Right. Only the small helper that opens the interface is privileged.

choices.text: A group member's capture loses fewer packets
choices.why: Who runs it changes nothing about how many packets arrive.

choices.text: Root cannot write pcap files in a home directory
choices.why: Root can write anywhere; that is the problem, not the benefit.

choices.text: The display filters only work for ordinary users
choices.why: Display filters work the same for anyone.

prompt: How many packets did the eight-second capture write to `files.pcap`?
hint: tshark printed the count when it stopped.

prompt: `files.pcap` was created with mode `-rw-------`. Why is that the right default for a capture file?
hint: What did the file contain?

choices.text: tshark cannot read a file other users can read
choices.why: tshark reads any file it has permission to; the mode protects the contents.

choices.text: It stops a second capture from writing into it
choices.why: A second capture run by ana could still write it; the point is who reads.

choices.text: It holds what crossed the wire, clear-text pages included
choices.why: Right. Anything readable on the wire is readable in the file.

choices.text: A private file takes less space on disk
choices.why: Permissions do not change a file's size.

prompt: A capture filter rejects a packet. What can you do about it afterwards?
hint: It acts before saving.

choices.text: Clear the filter and the packet reappears
choices.why: That is the display filter, which only hides.

choices.text: Find it in a separate file of rejected packets
choices.why: No such file is kept.

choices.text: Read it with `tshark -r` and no `-Y`
choices.why: Reading the file shows only what was recorded.

choices.text: Nothing: it was never recorded
choices.why: Right. The only remedy is a second capture.

prompt: Match each expression with where it works.
hint: Field names have dots in them.

pairs.right: A capture filter, or tcpdump: it is BPF
A display filter naming a field
A display filter only: BPF cannot see inside HTTP

right_distractors: Either bar, typed exactly the same

prompt: A web server returns an error about once an hour, and you want to see those responses. Which plan keeps the evidence?
hint: Which filter can lose a packet for good?

choices.text: A capture filter of `http.response.code >= 500`, so the file holds only failures
choices.why: That is a display filter's language; as a capture filter it is refused.

choices.text: Capture `tcp port 80` to a file, then display `http.response.code >= 500`
choices.why: Right. Wide enough to catch it, and narrowed afterwards as often as needed.

choices.text: Capture five minutes with `-a duration:300` and filter those
choices.why: An error once an hour is unlikely to fall inside five minutes.

choices.text: Capture `tcp port 443`, which is where web errors go
choices.why: Errors come back on whatever port the request used, and 443 is encrypted besides.

prompt: The Client Hello carried the site's name, `www.example.com`, in ___ although everything after it was encrypted.
hint: The opposite of encrypted.

prompt: `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0` found three frames in `files.pcap`. What were you counting?
hint: A SYN/ACK is the server's answer.

choices.text: Connections that failed to open
choices.why: A SYN alone says nothing about whether the answer came; all three did.

choices.text: Connections the client opened
choices.why: Right. The first packet of each: web1 on 80 and 443, web3 on 80.

choices.text: The servers' replies to the client
choices.why: Those carry ACK as well, so the filter excludes them.

choices.text: Packets that were sent twice
choices.why: A retransmission would be marked as one; these are three different ports and servers.

prompt: The display filter `port 80` was refused. What should have been typed?
hint: A display filter names a field.

choices.text: `port == 80`
choices.why: There is no field called port on its own; it belongs to a protocol.

choices.text: `tcp port == 80`
choices.why: Half BPF and half field: neither language reads it.

choices.text: `tcp.port == 80`
choices.why: Right. The protocol, a dot, the field, and a comparison.

choices.text: `"port 80"`, in quotes
choices.why: The quotes were already there for the shell; the words are the problem.

prompt: In the version recorded here, `ip.addr != 192.0.2.21` showed 18 packets. Which packets were they?
hint: It gave the same count as !(ip.addr == 192.0.2.21).

choices.text: Those with at least one address other than 192.0.2.21
choices.why: That is the older reading, and it matches nearly every packet, not 18.

choices.text: Those whose source was not 192.0.2.21
choices.why: That would include every request sent to web1.

choices.text: Those sent by 192.0.2.21 and nobody else
choices.why: That would be ip.src == 192.0.2.21, the opposite question.

choices.text: Those in which neither address was 192.0.2.21
choices.why: Right. 45 packets in the file, 27 to or from web1, 18 left.

prompt: A file holds 45 packets, and the conversation statistics count 27 to or from `192.0.2.21`. How many does `!(ip.addr == 192.0.2.21)` show?
hint: Every packet is either in the conversation or not.

prompt: A colleague captures on his own desk port with a correct filter for a server's traffic, records nothing, and writes in the ticket that the server sent nothing. What is the flaw?
hint: A correct filter in the wrong place.

choices.text: He should have captured without `sudo`
choices.why: Privilege decides whether the capture runs at all, and his did.

choices.text: His port could never have seen it, so an empty file proves nothing
choices.why: Right. On a switch, only a mirror port, a tap or the server itself sees that traffic.

choices.text: A display filter was hiding the packets
choices.why: The file itself was empty; a display filter cannot empty a file.

choices.text: The server's traffic was encrypted
choices.why: Encrypted packets are still captured; they are only unreadable.

prompt: Following TCP stream 0 printed the request and the page, ending in `served by web1`. What does that show about plain HTTP?
hint: Who else could have run that command?

choices.text: Anyone who copies the packets reads all of it
choices.why: Right. Headers and body cross the wire in clear text.

choices.text: Only the headers are readable; the body is compressed
choices.why: The body, served by web1, was printed as it was sent.

choices.text: It is readable only from a mirror port
choices.why: Anywhere the packets pass, a tap or the server itself, reads the same bytes.

choices.text: tshark decrypted it with the server's key
choices.why: There was nothing to decrypt.

prompt: Between `files` and `web1` the conversation table shows 15 frames, 1800 bytes one way and 12 frames, 3265 bytes the other. What explains the difference?
hint: Which side sent the pages?

choices.text: Three of the client's frames were lost on the way
choices.why: Nothing was lost; the counts come from what both sides sent.

choices.text: The mirror port dropped the server's copies
choices.why: The server's direction is the one with more bytes, not fewer.

choices.text: The server's answers carried the data; the client mostly sent requests and acknowledgements
choices.why: Right. More frames from the client, more bytes from the server: the shape of browsing.

choices.text: web1 retransmitted its answers
choices.why: A retransmission would add frames on web1's side, and it has fewer.

prompt: Which of these can the protocol hierarchy tell you? Choose all that apply.
hint: It counts frames per protocol, nothing else.

choices.text: That a protocol nobody expected is on the network
choices.why: Right: it is a line in the tree.

choices.text: Which page a client asked for
choices.why: That is a stream to follow, not a count.

choices.text: How many frames carried DNS
choices.why: Right: 4 in files.pcap.

choices.text: The round-trip time of each connection
choices.why: It has no times in it at all.

choices.text: What share of TCP carried HTTP or TLS
choices.why: Right: 4 and 8 of 37 frames.

prompt: Put the steps of an investigation with Wireshark in order.
hint: The only irreversible choices come first.
items: Choose a place that can see the traffic
Capture to a file with a broad capture filter
Narrow the view with display filters
trap: A display filter works on what was saved, so capturing has to come before it; and nothing is saved from a port that cannot see the traffic.

prompt: You must see the traffic between two servers on a switch, and all you have is a laptop on an ordinary port. What gets you the packets?
hint: What decides where a frame goes?

choices.text: Putting the laptop's interface in promiscuous mode
choices.why: Promiscuous mode accepts every frame that arrives, and the switch still sends none of theirs to that port.

choices.text: Running Wireshark as root on the laptop
choices.why: Privilege on the laptop changes nothing about what reaches its port.

choices.text: A display filter on the two servers' addresses
choices.why: It can only show what was captured, and none of it was.

choices.text: A mirror of one server's port to the laptop's
choices.why: Right. Or capture on one of the servers itself, lesson 12's way.
